strengths: Principled and novel problem formulation: The paper nicely formalizes the meta-active feature acquisition (meta-AFA) problem under retrospective missingness, connecting in-context learning via sequence models to sequential Bayesian experimental design.

Solid theoretical underpinning: The work provides clear causal identifiability conditions (MAR, exclusion restriction, positivity in Theorem 3.4) for CMI under missingness, and establishes surrogate optimality for greedy CMI in the sequence modeling / in-context setting (Theorem 4.2).

Amortized, retraining-free inference: Unlike standard AFA baselines that require expensive per-task retraining or unstable generative modeling/RL, L2M amortizes both uncertainty estimation and greedy policy selection in-context for unseen test tasks.

Comprehensive empirical and ablation study: The evaluation spans synthetic GPs, semi-synthetic BNN priors on real tabular features (Metabric, MiniBooNE, MIMIC-IV), and MNIST digit classification. The paper thoroughly analyzes calibration/coverage, varying context lengths, missingness rates, and includes static vs. adaptive policy ablations.
weaknesses: Marginal gains over static/random acquisition on real downstream tasks: As acknowledged in Section 5 and shown in Figures 4 and 12–13, the margin of adaptive L2M over random acquisition or static selection is relatively narrow on some real benchmarks (e.g., MIMIC readmission, MiniBooNE).

Baseline asymmetry due to meta-learning vs. task-specific training: The task-specific baselines (GDFS, DIME, DQN) are trained from scratch on small context sets, inevitably suffering from data scarcity. While this highlights the benefit of meta-pretraining, the paper lacks comparisons against meta-learning or transfer-learning baselines adapted to AFA.

Reliance on prior specification and domain alignment: As seen in Figure 8, generalization to real-world tasks depends heavily on how closely the synthetic BNN/GP pretraining prior matches the real task distribution. A systematic investigation into how prior misspecification affects downstream acquisition is limited.

Evaluation restricted to low-dimensional feature sets: Experiments are limited to $d \le 20$ candidate features. In many practical settings (e.g., full EHRs or high-throughput genomics), $d$ can be orders of magnitude larger, where transformer context length and combinatorial action spaces could become bottlenecks.

strengths: Novel and timely problem formulation: Formalizing meta-active feature acquisition (meta-AFA) as an in-context learning problem using sequence models is an elegant paradigm shift away from per-task generative modeling or task-specific reinforcement learning.

Principled theoretical framework: The paper provides clear identifiability conditions (MAR, Positivity, Exclusion Restriction) under retrospective missingness in Theorem 3.4 and establishes surrogate optimality for greedy CMI in Theorem 4.2, building nicely upon the foundations of Covert et al. (2023).

Effective architecture design: Adapting transformers for exchangeable context and partially observed features via custom masking (Figure 6) and permutation equivariance/invariance is technically sound and avoids ad-hoc imputation.

Comprehensive evaluation and transparency: The empirical evaluation across synthetic GP priors, semi-synthetic/real tabular benchmarks (MIMIC-IV, METABRIC, MiniBooNE), and MNIST demonstrates clear advantages in low-context and high-missingness regimes, accompanied by honest analyses of when adaptivity does and does not provide significant lift (e.g., Figures 12 and 13).
weaknesses: Limited dimensionality in empirical experiments: The experimental setup is restricted to relatively small feature spaces ($d = 10$ for tabular data, $d = 20$ pixel patches for MNIST). In many practical AFA applications (e.g., comprehensive clinical diagnostic panels, genomics), candidate feature dimensions can be much larger.

Marginal benefits of adaptivity over random/static selection on certain real-world datasets: On several benchmarks (such as MiniBooNE and MIMIC Readmission in Figures 4, 12, and 13), L2M's adaptive policy yields only marginal improvements over random acquisition or static ordering, largely driven by the quality of the underlying predictor rather than policy adaptivity.

Dependence on synthetic task priors: For classification, training relies on synthetic labeling functions drawn from Bayesian Neural Network (BNN) priors. As noted in Figure 8, out-of-distribution transfer to real-world tasks depends heavily on whether downstream tasks align with the pre-training prior, raising questions about generalizability across domains without domain-specific prior engineering.

strengths: Novel formulation of Meta-Active Feature Acquisition: Formalizing AFA across tasks as an in-context decision-making problem addresses a critical limitation of existing AFA methods, which require training a bespoke predictor and policy from scratch for every new task.

Principled integration of sequence modeling and uncertainty quantification: Using exchangeable Transformer sequence models to capture posterior predictive distributions and amortize uncertainty quantification under arbitrary retrospective missingness is conceptually elegant and connects nicely with recent advances in in-context Bayesian inference.

Formal grounding of retrospective missingness: The paper cleanly integrates missing data theory (MAR, exclusion restriction, positivity) and blocked policies to establish conditions under which the conditional mutual information (CMI) objective remains identifiable from retrospective observational data.

Comprehensive empirical scope: Experiments span synthetic Gaussian processes (including OOD Matern kernels), tabular medical and scientific benchmarks (MIMIC-IV, Metabric, MiniBooNE), and patch-based MNIST classification.
weaknesses: Learned policy barely outperforms random acquisition on realistic datasets: Looking at Figure 4, across almost all real and semi-synthetic datasets (Metabric, MiniBooNE, MIMIC Mortality, MIMIC Readmission, and MNIST), the acquisition trajectory of L2M is virtually indistinguishable from L2M (Random). This indicates that the active acquisition policy is providing little to no adaptive advantage over uniform random feature acquisition outside purely synthetic GP settings.

Conflation of predictor backbone strength with acquisition policy effectiveness: The large performance gap between L2M and prior baselines (GDFS, DIME, DQN, MLP) appears to stem almost entirely from the pre-trained Transformer sequence model being a vastly better in-context predictor than a 2-layer MLP trained from scratch on small samples. Because baselines are not provided with an equivalent pre-trained sequence backbone or meta-learning setup, it is impossible to attribute L2M's superiority to its feature acquisition mechanism rather than its predictive representation.

Myopic one-step surrogate: The policy optimization relies on a one-step-ahead greedy surrogate for CMI via Gumbel-Softmax relaxation. While computationally convenient, greedy acquisition is known to fail when features have complex combinatorial or synergistic interactions (e.g., parity/XOR relationships), limiting the claim of general sequential decision-making.

Notational errors in theoretical proofs: The appendix contains several typographical and indexing errors in the proofs. For instance, in Appendix A.1 (Proof of Theorem 3.4), line 2 incorrectly writes $p(Y, X_{t+1}(1) | X_t)$ instead of $p(Y, X_j(1) | X_t)$, and line 3 conditions on $R_{t+1} = 1$ rather than $R_j = 1$. In Appendix A.3, the change-of-measure step is redundant because queries are conditionally independent by Assumption A.5, making $p(Y^{(q)} | X_t^{(q)}, Z^{1:m}) / p(Y^{(q)} | X_t^{m+1:N}, Z^{1:m}) = 1$.

strengths: Original formulation: The paper introduces a novel framing of active feature acquisition (AFA) as an in-context decision-making problem via sequence modeling, removing the need for task-specific retraining and complex latent-variable generative modeling.

Principled treatment of missingness: The work establishes identifiability conditions (MAR, positivity, no direct effect) under a causal potential outcomes framework (Theorem 3.4), providing a theoretically grounded justification for acquiring features directly from retrospectively missing data without heuristic imputation.

Sound optimization objective: The authors formulate an end-to-end differentiable surrogate objective for conditional mutual information (CMI) acquisition and prove that its minimizer recovers the Bayes-optimal predictor and CMI-optimal acquisition actions (Theorem 4.2), which is efficiently optimized using straight-through Gumbel-Softmax pathwise gradients.

Thorough empirical evaluation: The empirical study is comprehensive, evaluating across synthetic tasks (GP, BNN), multi-step planning setups (BNN-Plan), and real-world tabular benchmarks (Metabric, MiniBooNE, MIMIC-IV, MNIST).

Extensive analysis and ablations: The appendix provides rigorous proofs, comparison against alternative meta-learning formulations (CNPs, test-time MAML fine-tuning), gradient estimator quality comparisons against IPW/REINFORCE, and calibration/coverage diagnostics.
weaknesses: Sensitivity to prior specification and covariate mismatch: For real-world benchmarks, pretraining relies on semi-synthetic label mechanisms over observed covariates. When trained on fully synthetic covariates and applied zero-shot to real tasks (L2M-Syn in Figure 14), the model experiences substantial degradation, demonstrating susceptibility to prior mismatch.

Marginal utility of instance-level adaptivity on certain tasks: The ablation in Figure 15 reveals that instance-adaptive acquisition performs comparably to a static majority-vote baseline on datasets like MiniBooNE and MIMIC-LOS/Readmission, indicating that dynamic acquisition does not always provide substantial gains over static feature ordering in these settings.

Dimensionality and sequence scaling limits: The evaluation is restricted to relatively low-dimensional feature sets (d ≤ 20) and context sizes up to 1000 samples. Sequence modeling over both feature dimensions and dataset contexts may encounter scalability bottlenecks in higher-dimensional tabular problems.

Minor typographical and referencing errors: There are several minor errors in the text, such as 'to access generalization' instead of 'assess' (page 7), 'We futher show' (page 9), and referencing 'Appendix 18' instead of 'Appendix A.8.5' (page 7).

strengths: Original and well-motivated problem formulation: The paper effectively bridges in-context learning (via transformer-based sequence modeling / PFNs) and active feature acquisition (AFA), enabling zero-shot or in-context feature acquisition on new tasks without requiring expensive per-task policy retraining.

Principled theoretical grounding: The authors provide rigorous causal identifiability conditions (MAR, positivity, no direct effect) for conditional mutual information (CMI) under retrospective missingness (Theorem 3.4) and prove surrogate loss optimality for sequence-level Bayes prediction and CMI-maximizing acquisition (Theorem 4.2).

Sound and flexible technical design: Formulating policy optimization with a straight-through Gumbel-Softmax relaxation enables end-to-end differentiable policy learning that seamlessly accommodates both myopic (greedy) and multi-step lookahead planning, supported by customized permutation-invariant attention masking.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Experiments span fully synthetic tasks (GPs, BNNs with interactions), semi-synthetic tabular benchmarks (Metabric, MiniBooNE, MIMIC-IV), and MNIST. The results demonstrate clear gains over task-specific baselines (GDFS, DIME, DQN), particularly under scarce context samples and high retrospective missingness.

Thorough ablations and diagnostics: The appendix includes valuable analyses on gradient estimator quality (pathwise vs. REINFORCE and IPW), uncertainty calibration/coverage, lookahead vs. greedy planning under feature synergies, and alternative meta-learning paradigms (such as CNP task pooling and MAML test-time fine-tuning).
weaknesses: Semi-synthetic reliance for real-world tabular data: In the primary real-world benchmark evaluations (Metabric, MiniBooNE, MIMIC-IV), pre-training utilizes the real dataset's covariate distribution paired with synthetic labels generated from a BNN prior. Although the authors evaluate a fully synthetic prior (L2M-Syn) in the appendix, performance notably degrades when transferring zero-shot across distinct covariate distributions, highlighting sensitivity to prior specification.

Simplified cost and budget structure: The formulation assumes uniform feature acquisition costs and a fixed step-budget horizon, whereas practical applications (particularly healthcare triage) often require cost-sensitive trade-offs with non-uniform costs and adaptive, state-dependent stopping rules.

Scalability to high feature dimensions: The evaluated tasks have relatively modest feature dimensions (d <= 20). Extending the sequence tokenization and joint masked representation to hundreds of continuous and categorical features may present computational bottlenecks for full-context attention.
Minor typographical errors: Minor typos appear in the manuscript (e.g., 'context datase' on page 4, 'futher' on page 9, and 'LTM' instead of 'L2M' in the caption of Figure 16).

strengths: Novel formulation of active feature acquisition (AFA) as an in-context learning problem via sequence models, effectively circumventing the need for per-task retraining or explicit generative latent-variable modeling.

Principled theoretical analysis that formalizes identifiability conditions under retrospective missingness (MAR, no direct effect, and positivity) and proves that the surrogate sequence loss recovers Bayes-optimal predictions and CMI-maximizing acquisition decisions.

Well-designed model architecture and training strategy, including attention masking tailored for context invariance and target equivariance, combined with straight-through Gumbel-Softmax relaxation to enable end-to-end gradient-based policy optimization.

Thorough empirical evaluation across diverse synthetic and semi-synthetic benchmark domains (GP, BNN, Metabric, MiniBooNE, MIMIC-IV, MNIST), supported by comprehensive ablations on gradient variance (vs. REINFORCE and IPW), lookahead planning, context lengths, and meta-learning architectures (e.g., CNP).
weaknesses: The evaluation on real-world datasets primarily relies on semi-synthetic task setups where labels are generated using synthetic BNN priors over real covariates; as shown in Section A.8.2 (L2M-Syn), performance noticeably degrades under fully out-of-distribution real covariate and label mechanisms without task-specific fine-tuning.

The test-time evaluation under real missingness patterns requires query instances to be complete cases for evaluation purposes, creating a distribution mismatch between partially observed context samples and fully available query ground-truth features.
The methodology is strictly restricted to time-invariant features, which limits immediate applicability to dynamic, longitudinal settings common in clinical monitoring and time-series environments.
